title: Local Lead Generation
subtitle: Help neighbours reach the right local business with a clear, trusted request.

blocks.text: A yard service needs customers, and a neighbour needs a hedge trimmed. Your job can be to help them find each other, without making the neighbour fill out a form that feels longer than the hedge.
Start with a clear match.
blocks.detail: A written lead definition helps you spend time on requests your client can serve, and makes your fee easy to defend.
blocks.extra: Section 05 shows you how to write the sorting rules and price the work.

blocks.text: A lead is a contact or request from someone who may need a service. It is not a promised sale. A qualified lead meets the rules you and your client agree on, such as the area, the service needed and permission to pass the request along.

This lesson covers a small service that brings clear local requests to one client business. You help that business receive and sort requests. You do not collect contact lists to sell to several buyers. The owner keeps control of the business page, prices and promises to customers. Start with a small trial so the owner can review the work before it grows.

sections.title: Build a path people can understand

blocks.text: Pick one service, such as routine yard care, and one area the client can cover. Ask the owner which jobs they take, when they have room and who will answer requests. A full calendar changes what your page should offer.

items.title: Publish a business page the owner approved, with the real service area and offer.
Invite people to a short request form. Others can share its public link.
Say who gets the request and why before you ask for permission.
Check the agreed lead rules, send the requests that fit and record each handoff.
Ask the client what happened with each lead, then report it.

blocks.text: Make your role clear. Say that you manage requests for the named yard service. Do not invent a local business, address or review to make the page look established.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC) says consent wording should clearly explain what you collect, who gets it and why. For this trial, name the client beside the permission box. Avoid a vague promise to share with “selected partners.”

items.title: “A public email address gives me permission to send any offer.”
items.text: The CRTC says a public address alone is not enough. You may rely on a published address only when its conditions are met, such as the message relating to the person’s job and no notice saying they don’t want offers. You must be able to prove it.

blocks.text: The CRTC says sales emails and texts generally need consent, the sender’s name and contact details, and a way to unsubscribe. An email asking for consent counts as a sales message too, so you need a lawful basis before you send it. Permission to answer one request does not cover later marketing.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: Owen’s Saturday slot

blocks.text: Owen’s Saturday slot
paragraphs: Owen lived in Hamilton and worked in a warehouse. He wanted to test a lead service on the side. A local yard-care owner had open Saturday slots but little time to sort messages. Owen offered a two-week trial for garden cleanup in one part of the city.

Their first public post brought in several requests, and Owen pictured a tidy report. Then a neighbour asked which company would show up. The page named the owner, but the form only said “a local provider” would call.

Owen paused the handoffs and showed the owner the gap. He could keep collecting requests under the vague wording. Or he could fix the form first. He chose to name the yard service right beside the sharing box, and the owner approved every step a customer would see.

He also added a question about the area and a note that the owner would confirm timing and price. Two neighbours who had used the old form sent a fresh request. Owen counted their first entries as replaced, not as extra leads.

Then came a surprise. Several good leads wanted weekday visits, not Saturdays. The owner could take some of those, but Saturday demand was weaker than they had hoped. They changed the next offer instead of blaming the people who replied.

The trial gave them a request process that worked and a clearer view of local demand. Owen’s report showed what the owner could serve and what needed to change. His Saturday idea had become a question they could test, not a promise he had to defend.

blocks.text: Walk through the whole path as a customer before launch. A clear post cannot fix a confusing form further down the page.
Trust makes the handoff easier.
blocks.detail: Clear names and plain expectations help people know who will contact them, and make them more likely to answer.
blocks.extra: Section 05 turns Owen’s fixes into a trial you can run.

blocks.text: This made-up example tests the process for two weeks. The sample fee is $240 plus tax, for one approved page, one form, sorting every weekday and a closing report. Ad spending is separate. This is a teaching example, not a market price.
Write the sorting rules first

The agreement says a qualified lead is one new household request for a job the client takes, inside the agreed area, with contact details that work and permission for the named client to receive it. Repeat entries for the same job count once. Agree how to dispute or replace a bad lead, and set the client’s reply target, such as one business day.
Agree who owns each step. Your handoff time and the client’s reply time are separate measures, and neither proves a booking happened.
Test the form and protect the records

Ask for a name, one way to make contact, the neighbourhood and a short job description. Let the business ask for the exact address when it needs it. OPC principles call for collecting only what you need, protecting it well and keeping it only as long as its purpose requires.

Limit access to the people who handle requests, use secure accounts and agree a deletion schedule with the client. Add a clear privacy contact. The OPC explains that PIPEDA, the federal privacy law, generally covers business personal information in Ontario. Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec have their own private-sector laws, and data that crosses borders can bring PIPEDA into play.

items.title: “Every form entry is a billable lead.”
items.text: Your agreed definition leaves out repeats, jobs the client does not do and other entries that miss the rules.

blocks.text: Reconcile the pilot report

In a second made-up report, there are 20 entries. Three are duplicates. Of the rest, two are outside the area and one is a job the client does not do. That leaves 14 qualified handoffs: 20 − 3 − 2 − 1 = 14. Six of those become appointments, so the appointment rate is 6 ÷ 14, about 43%. Appointments are not finished sales.
Give each number with its stage: 14 qualified handoffs, six appointments. Let the client confirm finished jobs separately.
Choose how you get paid

items.title: FLAT FEE
items.text: One set price for the trial or the month. Simple to bill, and you are paid for the work even in a slow week.

items.title: PRICE PER LEAD
items.text: A set amount for each qualified handoff. Works only when the lead rules are written down and both sides can check the count.

items.title: SHARE OF SALES
items.text: A cut of each job the client finishes. Hard for you to check, so leave it until you trust the client’s records.

items.title: TAX ON YOUR FEE
items.text: Your fee is business income for your tax return. Once your sales pass $30,000 in one quarter or over four quarters in a row, register for GST/HST and charge it.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Keep a short reason code for every entry you leave out. You can explain the totals without copying customer messages into each report.
Quick Check

items.title: Does a qualified lead guarantee a sale?
items.text: It meets your agreed inquiry rules, but the customer may decide not to book.

items.title: Should two entries for the same household job count twice?
items.detail: No, when your agreement excludes duplicates.
items.text: Keep one eligible request and label the repeat.

items.title: Who should approve the service area and offer?
items.text: They know which jobs they can take and remain responsible for their promises.

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: A client wants you to count all 12 entries, including four repeats for the same jobs. Your contract excludes duplicates. What should you report? A. Twelve qualified leads. · B. Eight unique requests, then check the other lead rules. · C. Four sales.
items.text: Remove repeats first; the eight remaining requests still need checks against the agreed criteria.

items.title: A homeowner asks for hedge trimming, but your client only offers lawn mowing. What should happen? A. Count a qualified handoff anyway. · B. Send the details to several other businesses. · C. Mark the job outside the agreed scope.
items.text: A genuine request can still be unsuitable for this client. Do not treat it as a qualified lead or quietly pass it elsewhere.

items.title: The owner wants a page that pretends your agency is a long-established yard service. What should you do? A. Use the client’s true identity and explain your inquiry role. · B. Invent reviews to support the story. · C. Hide who receives the requests.
items.text: A transparent page tells customers who provides the work and who manages inquiries.

items.title: Write one sentence describing a pilot you could test, including the service, area and the result you will measure.
items.text: I will test garden-cleanup requests in one Hamilton neighbourhood and count qualified handoffs separately from appointments.

blocks.text: Build one clear request path, agree what counts and report each stage honestly. Useful introductions begin with a need the client can serve.

Draft a one-paragraph trial offer from your answers. Include the work covered, how you will be paid and the client’s reply target. Then read the request page aloud to someone who has not seen it. Fix any wording that leaves them unsure who will contact them.

items.title: Lead
items.text: A contact or request from a possible customer.

items.title: Qualified lead
items.text: A request that meets the agreed rules.

items.title: Service area
items.text: The places a business has agreed to serve.

items.title: Handoff
items.text: Passing a request that fits the rules to the named client.

items.title: Duplicate
items.text: A repeat entry for the same request.

items.title: CASL
items.text: Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation, which sets rules for sales emails and texts.

quiz.question: A homeowner asks for hedge trimming, but your client only offers lawn mowing. What should happen?
choices: Send the details to several other businesses.
Mark the job outside the agreed scope.

questions: Which service and area will you cover?
What will make a request qualify for handoff?
How will the form tell people who will contact them?
How will you be paid for the trial?
Which numbers will your report show, and how will you keep them apart?
Which check will you do first, and when?
samples: Name one service and a neighbourhood or boundary. Leave out customer addresses.
Write the job, the area and the duplicate rule, plus how you will confirm permission to share.
For example: the yard service’s name beside the permission box.
Flat fee, price per qualified lead, or not sure yet.
For example: qualified handoffs, appointments and finished jobs, each counted on its own.
For example: test the form with a friend by Friday.
